translations.text: That is the fairest of joys when they meet at the beginning, the angel and the blessed soul!
She gives up the joys of this earth, abandons these transitory pleasures, and parts from the body.
Then the angel speaks (he has the higher rank), greets the other spirit, and announces God's message to him: "Now you may travel to the place you have long and often striven toward. I shall lead you.
The ways are pleasant for you, and the light of glory is brightly opened. You are now a traveller in due time to the holy home."

There sorrow never comes, nor turning back [?] because of miseries; but there is the joy of angels, peace and happiness, and the rest of souls. And there those who carry out his decrees here on earth may rejoice forever and make merry with the Lord.
He keeps eternal reward for them in heaven, where the highest King of all kings rules over the cities.
Those are the buildings that never decay, nor does life fail because of miseries for those who dwell there; rather, the longer it lasts, the better it is for them. They enjoy youth and God's mercies.
The souls of the righteous may come there after death, those who here teach and fulfil Christ's law and raise up his praise;

they overcome the accursed spirits and win for themselves the rest of glory. A man's mind must ascend there, sooner or later, when he tends his one spirit here, so that it may come, clean of sins, into the keeping of the Good One.
Many are the orders of life throughout the world under the heavens that rise up into the number of the holy.
We may rightly hear this of each one of them, if we are willing to keep the holy commandments. A wise man may now enjoy the blessing of good times and desire the way onward for his spirit.

The world is stirred up and Christ's love grows cold. Many temptations have arisen throughout the world, just as God's messengers said in words long ago and named it all through prophecy, as it now comes to pass.
The glory of the earth grows old in each of its excellences, and the natures of fruits turn away from their beauty; the later season of every seed is weaker in strength.
Therefore no one need expect from this world an improvement, that it will bring us fairer joy beyond the hostilities that we now endure,
before all the creatures come to an end that he established in six days, which now bring forth their kinds under the heavens, great and small. This world is divided into parts.
The Lord observes where those who keep his law dwell. He sees the decrees that he established through his own word diminish every day and turn away from what is right in the world.
He finds many; few are chosen.
Some want to carry the fame of that way of life in their words, and do not do the works.
To him earthly wealth is the highest of hopes, above eternal life, though that wealth must become estranged from every dweller on earth.

Therefore they now scorn the minds of the holy, those who fix their thoughts on heaven and know that the eternal homeland awaits all the multitude throughout the world who serve the Lord and desire that dear home according to their deeds.
So these worldly treasures are exchanged for the glorious goods when those over whose heads the fear of God hangs yearn for them.
They are chastened by the highest majesty; they enjoy this life according to the commandments, and they wish and hope for the better one hereafter.
They buy glory, give alms, comfort the poor, are generous with rightful treasures, love with gifts those who have less, and serve the Lord every day. He observes their deeds.
Some dwell in the wildernesses; of their own will they seek out and settle homes in dark places. They await the heavenly dwelling.
He who begrudges them life often brings hateful terrors upon them. He shows them frightening things, and sometimes vain glory; the crafty slayer is skilled in both, and he persecutes the hermits.
Angels stand before them, ready with spiritual weapons. They are mindful to help them, they guard the lives of the holy, and they know that their hope is with the Lord.
Those are the tried warriors who serve the King, who never withholds the reward from those who endure for his love.

We may now tell what has lately been made known to us through a holy person: how Guthlac directed his mind in God's will, scorned all wickedness and earthly nobility, and fixed his thoughts on the home in heaven above.
His hope lay in this, after he who prepares the way of life for souls had enlightened him and given him angelic grace,
so that he alone began to dwell in a hill-dwelling, and through humility gave all his glory to God, the glory he was meant to have spent in his youth on the joys of the world.
A holy guardian from heaven watched over him, who eagerly strengthened that pure mind in the goodness of the spirit.
Lo, we have often heard that the holy man, in his earliest years, loved many dangerous deeds!
Yet a time was set in God's judgement when an angel granted Guthlac in his understanding that the desires for sin should weaken in him.
The time was approaching. Two guardians watched over him and carried on a struggle: an angel of the Lord and the terrible spirit.
Many times they brought very different teaching into the thoughts of his mind.
One told him that all this earth under the sky is passing, and praised the lasting goods in heaven, where the souls of the holy sit in victorious glory amid the joys of the Lord;
he eagerly repays the reward for their deeds to those who will receive his gifts with thanks and put this world further from them than the eternal life.

The other urged him to seek out gangs of robbers by night and, through daring deeds, strive after worldly gain, as outlaws do who care nothing for the life of the man who brings plunder into their hands, so long as they may possess the spoil.
So they urged him from both sides, until the Lord of hosts brought that struggle to an end in the angel's favour.

The fiend was put to flight. After that the Spirit of comfort stayed to help Guthlac. He loved him and taught him, the longer the more earnestly, so that the joys of that land, the dwelling on the hill, became dear to him.

Often terror came there, dreadful and strange, the hostility of the ancient foes, strong in cunning crafts; they showed themselves to him in their own form, and they had once occupied many dwellings there.
From there they made their journey, wandering far and wide, cut off from glory, flying through the air. That place in the land was hidden from men until the Creator revealed a hill in the woods,

Then the builder came who raised a holy home there. He did not do it because he cared, out of greed, for the wealth of this passing life. Instead he made that land a fair sanctuary for God, after Christ's warrior had overcome the fiend.

He was tested within the lifetimes of men who still remember, who even now honour him because of spiritual wonders and keep up the fame of his wisdom: that the holy servant, with courage, achieved this when he alone settled in a hidden place.

There he spoke and raised up the Lord's praise. Often, in speech, he proclaimed God's messages to those who loved the ways of those who suffer for God, when the Spirit revealed to him the wisdom of life,
so that he denied his body its pleasures and worldly delights, soft seats and feast-days, and also the pleasures of idle eyes and showy clothing.
The fear of God was greater in his mind than any wish he had to take part in human splendour as he pleased.

Guthlac was good! He carried a heavenly hope in his spirit and reached the salvation of eternal life. An angel was near him, a faithful guardian of peace, for he was one of the few who settled in the borderland.
where he became an example to many in Britain, once the blessed champion, hard in battle, had climbed the hill.
He armed himself eagerly with spiritual weapons and blessed the plain. As his battle-station he first set up Christ's cross, where the champion overcame many dangers.
Many of God's martyrs became strong. We declare that Guthlac's precious share came from the Lord.
He gave him victory and the power of wisdom, and protection by his might, whenever a crowd of fiends came with sudden shots to stir up hostility.

They could not give up their malice, but brought many temptations to Guthlac's spirit. Help was near him: the angel strengthened him with courage whenever they threatened him in anger, fiercely, with the surge of fire.
They stood around him in troops and said that he would burn on the hill, and the flame would swallow his body, so that all his suffering would come upon his kinsmen as grief of heart,
unless he himself would turn back from that warfare and seek out the joy of men again, and willingly keep his rightful bond of kinship with mankind with greater care, and let his exile rest.

So the one who spoke for the whole crowd of fiends raged at him. Guthlac's spirit was none the more afraid, but God gave him courage against that terror, so that the guilty band of the ancient enemy suffered shame;

The makers of affliction were full of rage. They said that Guthlac alone, together with God himself, had brought the greatest of hardships upon them, since out of pride he had broken into the hills in the wilderness, where they, while waiting,

wretched adversaries, had once been allowed to enjoy times of rest after their torments, when they came weary from their wanderings to rest for intervals in their course and rejoiced in the peace; that had been granted to them for only a little while.
The secret place stood in the Lord's remembrance, unused and empty, far from any rightful owner, awaiting the claim of a better keeper.
At that the ancient foes took offence, just as they constantly suffer sorrow.

They may not enjoy a dwelling on earth, nor does the air lull them to sleep with rest for their limbs. Instead, without shelter, they go without homes; in their sorrows they lament, they long for death, and they want the Lord to clear a way through the agony of death to the end of their hardships.

They could not harm Guthlac's spirit, nor separate soul from body with painful blows, but with lying tricks they raised up words of harm, set aside their laughter, and lamented their sorrows, when the stronger guardian overcame them on that ground.
The exiles had to give up the green hills, lamenting.

Yet even then the adversaries of God spoke with bitter words and solemnly vowed that he would have to suffer the parting of death if he waited any longer for a more hateful meeting, when they would come with a greater multitude, who would care little for his life.
Guthlac answered them back. He said that they had no reason to boast of their deeds against the might of the Lord.
"Though you threaten me with death, he who rules over your constraints will save me from those attacks.
There is one almighty God, who can easily shield me; he will protect my life. I will tell you many truths. I alone, without hardship, can wrest this seat from you.
I am not as lacking in a band of men as I seem, standing before you; rather, a greater force dwells and grows in me through divine spiritual mysteries, and it protects me against hostility.
Here I will easily build myself, alone, a house and a shelter; my teachings depend on heaven. I have little doubt that an angel will lead me to all prosperous success in words and deeds.
Go now, accursed ones, weary in spirit, from this place on which you stand here; flee far away."
I will seek peace for myself from God; my spirit shall not suffer error along with you, but the Lord's hand protects me with might. Here shall be my earthly home, no longer yours."
Then a clamour was raised. The exiles stood in throngs around the hill. Fury rose up, the cry of the wretched. Many called out, spokesmen of the fiends, and boasted wickedly:
"Often we have watched, between the seas, the ways of nations and the violence of proud men, those who ruled their lives in good fortune.
Never have we found greater arrogance in a single man anywhere in the world.
You declare that you will take a home from us, you who are God's wretch.
What will you live on, even though you possess the land?
No one will feed you here with food; hunger and thirst will be harsh enemies to you if you leave your homeland alone like a wild beast. That undertaking is worth nothing!
Give up this seat! No one can teach you better counsel than this whole multitude.

We will be gracious to you if you will obey us; otherwise we will come at you again, when you are unprepared, with a greater force, so that no one will need to touch you with hands, nor will your corpse fall by the wounds of weapons.
We can trample this dwelling down with our feet; a host will press in with troops of horses and bands of men.
Those who will trample you down will be enraged; they will tread on you and torment you, and wreak their anger, and carry you off with bloody tracks;
If you intend to wait for us, we will assail you with hostility. Begin to seek a refuge; go where you expect to find friends, if you care for your life."
Guthlac was ready; God supported him in his answer, and he was strong in courage.

He did not flinch at their words but told his adversaries of sorrow, and made the truth plain enough to them: "Wide is this wilderness, with many places of exile, hidden dwellings of wretched spirits.
Those who inhabit these dwellings are breakers of faith.
Even if you summon them all out, and make yourselves a wider strife as well, here in this vengeful attack you will bring upon yourselves a journey without victory.

I do not intend to bear a sword against you with an angry hand, a weapon of the world; this plain shall not be settled for God through bloodshed. Instead I intend to please my Christ with a dearer offering.

Now that I have climbed up to this land, you have offered me many dwelling places through empty words. My heart is not fearful or doomed, but he who rules over every power by his works keeps me in peace, beyond the race of men.
Nothing dear to me depends on you, nor may you do me any harm. I am the Lord's servant; he often comforts me through an angel.
Therefore cares [?] seldom come upon me or bring me sorrow, now that a guardian of souls watches over me.
My hope is in God. I do not care at all for earthly wealth, nor do I yearn in my mind for much; instead, every day the Lord sends me what I need through the hand of man."

So the champion of glory showed courage, he who stood against the multitudes, worthily supported by the might of angels. The whole host of fiends departed from there. The respite that they meant to grant Guthlac was not long.
He was courageous and humble. He waited on the hill (he needed a dwelling) and gave up longing for passing joys.
He did not withhold his kindness from men, but prayed for the well-being of every soul when he bowed his face to the ground in that solitude. From heaven his heart was inspired with a joyful spirit.
Often he considered (an angel was near him) how he could enjoy the pleasures of this world as little as possible with his body.

His faith never wavered for fear of the wretched spirits. Nor did he neglect the hour of what he had to do for his Lord, so that the slumber of sleep or a sluggish mind might at any point [?] rob him of his zeal.
So a warrior must always fight for God in his mind, and often turn his spirit in hostility against the one who wants to hunt down every soul he can catch.

Always they found Guthlac steadfast in God's will when, fierce in flight, they came through the mists of night to visit him, those who had guarded those hidden dwellings; yet their delight in that place dwindled;
[?] they wanted sorrow, out of love for people, to come into his mind, so that he would turn his journey back to his homeland.

That attempt did not succeed, since the angel greeted him most eagerly in that solitude and gave him grace, so that longing could not keep him from the will of the Creator. Instead he remained in the covenant of the teacher.
Often he said in words: "Truly, he has need of this, the one whom the Holy Spirit guides in will and whose work he strengthens,
[?] invites him with gentle words and promises him the rest of life, so that he will obey the teachings of the guide and not let the old enemy afterwards turn his mind away from his Creator.
How will my spirit come to help, unless I give God an obedient mind, so that the thought of his heart may come to an end sooner or later, so that you may carry me off to [?] a wonder?
My body cannot escape death in this passing created world. It must perish, like all this earth that I stand on here.
Even if you, fierce-minded, seize my flesh with the surge of fire, with greedy flame, you will never turn me from these words as long as my wits last.
Though you assail it with pains, you may not touch my soul; instead you will bring it into a better place. Therefore I will wait for what my Lord decrees for me. I have no sorrow about that death.
Though my bones and blood both become an increase to the earth, my eternal part will go into joy, where it will enjoy a fairer dwelling.
The seat on this hill is no more splendid or greater than suits a man who daily carries out the Lord's will in sufferings.
The Lord's servant must not love earthly wealth in his heart beyond his own measure, only enough to have sustenance for his body."
Then, as before, the malice of the ancient fiends and their strife was stirred up again. One raged, another sang out [?] not a little, when the clamour of the sorrowful spirits rose into the air.
The praise of Christ always grew and remained in Guthlac's good mind, and the God of hosts protected him on earth, just as he keeps every living being safe where its spirit thrives in virtues.
He was one of those; he did not strive after worldly things, but raised the joy of his mind up into glory. Who was greater than he?
A single warrior, a champion in our times, makes known that Christ showed him more wonders than many worldly men [?].
He shielded him against the terrible grips of the harmful, wretched spirits. They were fierce in rushing at him with greedy grasps.
God did not wish the soul to suffer pain in the body because of this. Nevertheless he allowed them to touch him with their hands, and protection against them was secured.
Then they raised him into the high air and gave him power over mankind, so that he saw everything before his eyes: the conduct of men in monasteries under the authority of holy shepherds,
of those who spend their lives in pleasure, in idle possessions and excess, in showy clothing, as is the habit of youth when fear of the elder does not restrain it.

The fiends had no cause to rejoice there. They had quickly used up the success they were allowed for a little while, and they could no longer torment his body with punishments. Nothing they had done to injure him harmed him at all.
Then they led him from the air to the dearest dwelling-place on earth, so that he climbed the hill in the grove again.

The slayers lamented. Grieving, they bewailed that a son of man had overcome them by force [?], and that he had come alone, so needy, to cause them hardship, if they could not repay him for their grief with greater pains in vengeance.
Guthlac set his hope in the heavens and trusted in salvation; he had come through the grip of the fiends with his life.
The first temptation by the wretched spirits was overcome. The warrior lived happily on the hill; his glory was with God.

It seemed to him in his mind that the man among mankind is blessed who protects his own life here, so that the fiend's hand does not harm him at the very end, when the Lord's judgment guides him to the last, inevitable parting.

Yet the slanderers, still mindful of their injuries, threatened him with miseries in angry, insulting words. His faith was made manifest, and God rewarded Guthlac's courage with honours, which he alone had won.

The accursed spirit spoke to him in words: "We would not have needed to afflict you so severely if you had been willing to promptly obey the teachings of friends, when you first came, lowly and poor, into this warfare,
when you promised that the Holy Spirit would easily shield you against hardships, because of the mark [the tonsure] by which a man's hand took away the nobility of your appearance.

In that guise many live who are given over to sins. They by no means partake of good things; instead, out of love, they please their bodies with the joys of feasting. In this way you pay honour to the Lord in foolish revelry.
You hide from men many of the things you devise in your mind, but your deeds are not hidden, even though you do them in secret.
We led you into the air and deprived you of the joys of the land. We wanted you to see for yourself that we accused you truly.
You have earned punishment for all of this, because you could not change it."
Then it had come to pass that God wished to reward him with thanks after his sufferings, because he loved martyrdom in his mind. He gave him wisdom in the thoughts of his heart, a steadfast mind.
He stood against many of the ancient foes, made bold by courage, and told them, to their sorrow, that they must give up the green plain without victory: "You are condemned; guilt rests upon you!
"You do not know how to ask the Lord for glory, nor how to seek grace with humility, though he permitted you for a little while to have power over me.
You would not accept that patiently, but angrily you led me up, so that I could see the buildings of the lands from the air. The light of heaven was opened bright to me, though I suffered affliction.
You reproached me because I easily tolerated lax rules and the fierce temper of young men in God's temples.
By that you wished to scorn the praise of the holy. You sought out the worse, and did not judge the better according to their deeds. Those deeds are not hidden, nevertheless.
I will tell you the truth hereafter:
God created youth and the joy of men. Later ages cannot bring forth the first glory, but they delight in the pleasures of the world until the count of winters comes upon youth,
the spirit loves the bearing and nature of an older state of life, which many throughout the world serve with moderation in their customs.
Men show wisdom to the peoples and lose their pride once the spirit flees the folly of youth.
That you do not make clear. Instead you tell of the sins of the guilty, and you do not want to proclaim the minds and conduct of the righteous.
You rejoice in crimes. You do not expect the comfort of living to see your exile relieved.
You often stand in thefts [?]; for that, punishment will come from heaven."
Then he who can judge us will send me victory, he who rules the length of every life."
So spoke the holy warrior. The martyr was set apart from the sins of mankind. Still he had to endure a share of pain, though the Lord controlled his torments.
Lo, it seemed a wonder to men that he would let the wretched spirits touch him further with fierce grips, and yet that happened!

That was greater still: that he himself came to the earth and shed his blood at the hands of slayers. He had power over both life and death when he willingly and humbly endured the hatred of persecutors on earth.

It is therefore right and honourable now that we give judgement on the deeds of the devout, and speak praise to the Lord for all the examples that books set before us, making wisdom known to us through the work of his wonders.
Grace was found in Guthlac, through divine power. It is a great deal to tell everything from the beginning, all that he endured with courage:
the almighty Father himself set that champion against hidden deadly foes, and there his soul became pure and was tested.
It is widely known throughout the world that his mind thrived in God's will. There is still much more to tell of what he himself endured in the tight fetters of hostile spirits.

He scorned those pains. His soul was always kept well by the protector who guarded his mind, so that the faith in his breast never wavered, and no grief harmed his spirit. His firm mind remained holy until he had outlasted that trouble.
The afflictions were harsh and the servants fierce; all of them promised him the loss of his life.
Yet those guardians of sins were not allowed to condemn him to death, and his soul waited in his body for a better time.

They saw clearly that God meant to save him from their hostility and to judge their violent persecution severely. In this way the Lord, who alone is almighty, can easily shield any of the blessed against hardship.

Even so, the enraged and wrathful outcasts brought the champion of glory, the holy child of the Eucharist, to the door of hell. That is where the doomed spirits of the wicked, after their death-agony, first seek entry into that terrible house, down beneath the headlands into the deep abysses.
They terrified him and threatened war. They showed terror and malice without mercy and made fierce threats, as fiends do when they want to trap the soul of the righteous with sins and cunning tricks.

Hostile-hearted, they began to torment God's warrior in his mind. They vowed fiercely that he would have to go into that grim terror, go humiliated to the dwellers of hell, and suffer burning there in bonds.
The wretched monsters wanted to drag the Creator's champion into despair with bitter words. It could not be so!

The anxious ones, hateful to Christ, spoke fiercely to Guthlac: "You are not worthy. You are not a servant of the Lord who has been purely tested, nor a good warrior well proven in words and works, nor holy in heart."
"Now you must plunge deep into hell. You will never have the Lord's light in the heavens, the lofty buildings, a seat in the sky, because you committed too many sins and crimes in the flesh.
We will now pay you back for every sin, in the place most hateful to you, in the grimmest torment of the spirit."

The blessed man Guthlac answered them in spirit, with God's power: "Go ahead, then, if the Lord Christ, the author of the light of life and the ruler of hosts, will allow you to lead his servant into that hateful fire.
That lies in the power of the King of glory, Christ the Saviour, who humbled you and drove you into captivity, into tight fetters.
I am his humble attendant, a patient servant. I must accept his sole judgement of all things everywhere, and with eager spirit and mind I will be subject to him forever,
loyally obey my Saviour's ways and counsels, and thank him for all the gifts that God created, first for the angels and then for the dwellers on earth;
and with a joyful mind I bless the source and light of life, and sing praise to him with fitting judgement day and night, and praise the guardian of the heavenly kingdom in my heart.

so that you will never be permitted from above, by the favours of light, to speak praise to the Lord. Instead, in death you must lament the surging woe with weeping, wailing in hell, and never have the holy praises of the King of heaven.
In my days I will honour that judge with words and deeds and love him in life, since teaching and honour are thus brought to prosperous speech for the one who carries out his will in his works.

You are oath-breakers, since you have long lived in exile, sunk in flame, darkly deceived, deprived of heaven, bereft of joy, given over to death, bound by sins, without hope of life, that you found a remedy for blindness.
In days long past you readily scorned the fairer creation, the spiritual joy of God, when you turned against the holy Lord.

You were not allowed to live forever in days of joy. Instead, because of your pride, you were thrust in shame and guilt into eternal fire, where you must endure death and darkness and weeping forever. You will never know any relief from it.
And I believe in the source of life, the eternal ruler of all creation, that he, the Saviour from afflictions, in his mercy and his great might,
will never abandon me because of my brave deeds. I have long fought for him as God's warrior, in my body and in my spirit, through the mysteries of many powers.

Therefore I trust in the most radiant majesty of the Trinity, who by his will holds heaven and earth in his hands, that you will never be able to drag me into torments with your hatred and anger, you my murderers and wicked destroyers, dark and defeated."
Truly I am filled fairly in my breast with bright faith and with love of the Lord, my heart stirred toward the better home, my limbs lit up toward the dearest eternal homeland,

There is a homeland, fair and joyful, in the glory of the Father. There the Saviour will never give you the gleam of light or the hope of life in God's kingdom, because of the arrogance that rose up in your minds, all too strongly, through vain boasting.
In your defiance you thought and wished that you would be equal to the Creator in glory.

It went worse for you there, when the Ruler angrily sank you into that black torment. There a fire mixed with poison was later kindled for you, and by a deep judgement your joy, the fellowship of the angels, was taken away.
So it shall now be forever and ever: you shall have the burning surge of damnation [?], not blessings.

You who are cut off from glory need not expect that you sinners may use cunning arts to shove me shamefully under the shadow, or fling me back into the blaze of the pyre, into the house of hell. A home has been made for you there: black, endless night, strife without end, grim torment of the spirit.

There you shall suffer death in mourning, and I shall have the bliss of joys with the angels in the lofty kingdom of the heavens. There is the rightful King, help and salvation to the human race, glory and fellowship."
Then the Lord's messenger came, holy, from the heavens. With his voice he proclaimed a fear from on high to the wretched spirits.
he soon commanded that the innocent warrior of glory be led back from exile sound of limb, so that the dearest spirit, made ready in God's covenant, went forth in joy.
Then the troop of fiends grew terrified at that fear. The glorious one spoke, the dear thegn of the Lord, shining as bright as day.
The courageous protector, abundant in powers, had Guthlac's spirit in his keeping. He bound the thegns of darkness with harsh constraints, laid compulsion on them, and commanded urgently:

"Let him suffer no breaking of bones and no bloody wound, no bruise to his body and no harm at all of the kind you could do to injure him. Instead, you shall set him down unharmed in the place where you took him.
He shall rule that plain, and you may not keep that dwelling from him.
I am the judge whom the Lord commanded to declare swiftly that you should heal each of his wounds with your hands, and afterwards be obedient to him according to his own judgement.
I shall not hide my face before your multitude. I am the Creator's thane.
I am one of the twelve, the most faithful, whom he loved in his heart while in human form.
He sent me here from heaven. He saw that on earth you had, out of envy, inflicted torment on the one under his protection.
That is my brother; his trouble grieved me.
Now that I may help him, I shall bring it about that you will often see my face where this friend dwells in that refuge, he with whom I wish to keep that peace."
Now I will visit him often; I shall bring his words and his works before the Lord as witness. He knows his deeds."
Then Guthlac's spirit was gladdened, once Bartholomew had announced God's message.
The obedient captives stood ready and hardly disregarded the holy man's words. Then the glory-blessed warrior of the Lord began to make the welcome journey to the desired part of the earth.
They carried him and kept him from breaking. They lifted him with their hands and protected him from falling.
Under the fear of God their going was smooth and gentle. The builder came, victorious, to the hill.
Many kinds of creatures, the offspring of the tree-birds, blessed him with eager voices. By their signs they made known the blessed man's return.
He often held out food for them when they flew hungry around his hand, eager and ravenous, rejoicing in the help.
So that gentle spirit parted itself from the joys of mankind and served the Lord. After he had scorned this world, he took his delight in the wild creatures.

The plain of victory was calm and the dwelling new. The voices of the birds were fair and the earth was in bloom; cuckoos announced the year. Guthlac, blessed and resolute, was allowed to enjoy the dwelling.
The green plain stood in God's protection. The shepherd who came from the heavens had driven away the fiends.
What fairer wish has been fulfilled in the life of men, among those that our elders remembered or that we ourselves have known since?
Truly, we are witnesses of these wonders!
All these things happened in our own time. Therefore no one of the human race on earth need doubt
but God works such things to strengthen the life of souls, so that weak minds need not doubt the testimony when they enjoy the truth before their own eyes.
how the Almighty loves all creation under the sky in bodily form, the race of men throughout the world.

The Ruler wishes us always to take in wisdom with understanding, so that his truth may become current among us in payment for his gifts, which he gives and sends us for our benefit and understanding. He opens to souls gentle paths of life, brightly directed.
It is by no means the least of the things that love makes known when it builds spiritual gifts in a person's mind, as he raised up Guthlac's days and deeds through his judgment.
His beginning was firm, set against the fiends and against sins. Afterwards, there, he seldom fell short in his covenant [?]. He often sent his words up to God in humility,
and let his prayer come into that bright creation. He thanked the Prince that he was allowed to wait amid sufferings until a better life would be given to him by God's will.
So Guthlac's spirit was carried up into heaven in the arms of angels. They led it lovingly before the face of the eternal Judge.

He was given his reward: a seat in heaven, where he may always, for ever and ever, live settled and wait in bliss. The Son of God is his gentle protector, the mighty Lord, the holy shepherd, guardian of the kingdom of heaven.

In the same way the souls of the righteous may climb up into the eternal dwelling, the kingdom of the heavens. These are the people who here carry out, in word and deed, the enduring teaching of the King of glory. In their lifetime on earth they earn eternal life, a home on high.
These are the men of the Eucharist, chosen warriors, dear to Christ. They carry bright faith and holy hope in their hearts, and with pure hearts they honour the Ruler.
They have a wise mind, eager for the journey onward to the Father's homeland. They prepare the house of the spirit. With wisdom they fight down the fiend and hold back sinful desires in their hearts.
They eagerly practise brotherly fellowship, toil hard in God's will, adorn the soul with holy thoughts, and carry out the command of the King of heaven on earth.
They love fasting, guard themselves against wicked malice, and seek out prayer. They labour against sins and hold to truth and right.
They will not regret it after they depart, when they go into the holy city and go straight to Jerusalem, where they may eagerly gaze on the face of God in joy for ever,
peace and vision, where it truly dwells, beautiful and glorious, for all eternity in the joy of the land of the living.
It is widely known among the generations of men and famous among the peoples that God of the beginnings, the almighty King, made the first of the human race from the purest earth.
Then came a new beginning of the human race, a delightful foundation, fair and joyful. Adam, the father, was first brought forth by God's grace in paradise, where he lacked nothing he desired,
nor was there any decay of wealth, loss of life, or fall of the body, no failing of joy or coming of death. Instead he could live in that land free of all sins and long enjoy new delights.

where he would not have needed to await an end of life or of joys in that bright home through the ages, but after a time they would have been allowed to pass to the most beautiful joy of the heavenly kingdom, limbs and body together with the spirit of life,

And there they could have lived ever after in everlasting joys, for all time, in the sight of the Lord, free from death from then on, if they had been willing to keep the Holy One's word bright in their hearts, obey his commands, and carry them out in their homeland.

Too soon they grew weary of doing the Ruler's will. Instead his wife, taught by the serpent, took the forbidden fruit, and against God's word she plucked from the tree the fruit that had been forbidden to them.
of the King of glory, and through the devil's cunning she gave her husband a death-bearing morsel that drew the wedded pair to their death.

After that, the homeland was lost to Adam and Eve, the best of dwellings, bright, snatched away, and so it was for their children and their offspring after them, when they were driven out into an unknown place, hurrying in shame, thrust into the world of strife.
Through death's slaughter they paid for the deed, for the deep sins they had foolishly committed before.
For that sin's punishment, women and men afterward had to pay for the crime: a sorrow of guilt before God, through the parting of the soul from the body, for deep sins.
Death pressed in upon the race of men, and the fiend reigned throughout the world. Never afterwards was any man of that victorious stock so eager for God's will,
[?] nor so widely learned that he can escape the bitter drink that Eve, the young bride, long ago gave Adam, serving as cupbearer. That harmed them both in that precious home.
Death reigned over the dwellers on earth, though there were many holy in spirit who did God's will in various dwellings of men, in places across the land.

Some earlier, some later, and some within the memory of our own times, as time is reckoned, sought the reward of victory. Books tell us how, by God's will, Guthlac became blessed in England. He chose eternal might and protection for himself.

His wonderful works became famous far and wide, renowned in towns throughout Britain: how, by God's might, he often healed many who were troubled in mind by heavy torments. Bound by disease, they came to him sad at heart, sorrowful and in pain, from distant roads.
There with God's warrior they always found comfort ready, help and healing.
No man can tell, or knows the number of, all the wonders that he performed here in the world for the people by the Lord's grace.
Often the deadly host of devils, cut off from blessings, came to those dwellings in troops, thronging in bands, where the holy servant, resolute in courage, guarded his home.

There, in many different voices, they raised a loud war-cry in frenzy in the wilderness, stripped of their form and cut off from joys. The Lord's champion, the bold leader of the people, stood firm against the troops of fiends.
The time was not slow in coming for the wretched spirits, nor was the wait long, before the makers of crime raised up weeping, cried out without glory, and clamoured with their voices.

At times they raged like wild beasts and shrieked in a throng. At times the [?] wicked evildoers turned back into human form with the greatest uproar. At times the accursed traitors changed again into the shape of a serpent, and the wretched fire-maimed ones spewed poison.
They always found Guthlac ready and wise in thought. He waited patiently, though the band of fiends threatened him with death.
At times, driven by hunger, the race of birds flew to his hand, where they found sure food, and they honoured him with eager voices.
At times human messengers came to him again in humility, and there on that field of victory the travellers found help from the holy servant, and comfort for the spirit.
So there was never anyone who went away again ashamed, downcast and without hope. Instead, through that noble power, the holy man healed every one of those who came to him sick and in need,
men sad in mind. He healed both body and soul, for as long as the Guardian of life, eternal and almighty, was willing to grant that he might enjoy prosperity here, the life of the world.

Then the final day of his miseries and struggle on earth was pressed close by the parting that must come. He had chosen a dwelling in the wilderness fifteen years before, when the Spirit of comfort, holy from on high, was sent down from above to the blessed messenger.
His heart burned within him, eager for the journey forth. Suddenly sickness came into him. Even so, he waited courageously and undismayed, joyful in his dwelling, for the bright promises.
After the gloom of night, the bone-chamber was nearly overwhelmed and the treasure of his breast assailed. The joyful spirit was eager for the journey forth.

The Father of angels would not let him stay any longer in the life of this unhappy world, free of sins as he was, since he had pleased Him here with works and deeds during the time of his days, never slack in zeal.
Then the Almighty let His hand come to where the holy servant waited in seclusion, brave-minded, glorious, hardy and courageous.
Hope was renewed, and bliss in his breast. His bone-chamber was set on fire by sickness and held fast in inner bonds. The hoard of the body was unlocked. His limbs grew heavy, afflicted by pains.
He knew the truth: that the Almighty, the Measurer, was visiting him from above out of mercy. He firmly strengthened his mind against the sudden assault of the fiends' attacks.

Yet he was not afraid. Neither the onslaught of sickness nor the parting of death troubled his mind. Instead, praise of the Lord burned in his breast, and a burning-hot love, victorious in his heart, which always overpowered every pain for him.

He felt no sorrow or care in this passing time, though his body and spirit, the wedded pair, were dearly parting their life together. The days glided onward, and the darkness under the coverings of night.

The time was near when he had to fulfil the ancient deed through the coming of death and receive judgement: the very same that our ancestors suffered perilously long ago, as the first of the human race had brought it about before them.
Then in that grievous time Guthlac's strength was worn down, but his mind was very firm, resolute in courage. The illness was severe, hot and fiercely grim.
His heart surged within him, and the locker of his bones burned. The brew had begun that Eve brewed for Adam at the beginning of the world.
The fiend poured it first for the woman, and then she poured the bitter cup for Adam, her dear husband.
Because of that, their children afterwards paid the tribute grimly for that ancient deed, so that from the beginning there has been no one of the human race, no man on earth,
who could save himself and avoid the pale drink of the deep cup of death. Instead, at that cruel time, the door itself soon opens for him and lays the entrance open.
No one enclosed in flesh, mighty or lowly, can withstand it and keep his life; it rushes upon him with greedy grips.
So then, after the shadow of night, the fierce lone-goer, the slaughter-greedy warrior, was brought close at hand to Guthlac. A single attendant lived with him and visited him every day.

Then the deep-minded one, wise of heart, set out to go to God's temple, where he knew the herald of the heavenly homeland was inside, the dearest chosen teacher. He went in to speak with the blessed one, wanting to hear the holy man's teachings and the gentle one's words.
Then he found his lord weary with sickness. That fell heavy on his heart. He carried sorrow of mind and great anguish of heart. Then the young retainer began to ask:
"How has this come upon you, my friend and lord, father, protector of friends, your spirit troubled and hard pressed? Dearest lord, never before have I found you so weary.
Can you still command your words in speech? I expect that weakness, through the assaults of disease, has afflicted you this last night, and painful wounds have come upon you."
That is the hottest of sorrows in my breast until you comfort my mind and spirit. Do you know, noble lord, how this sickness will end?"

Then the one already setting out on his journey answered him. He could not draw breath at once; a bitter sickness had bent its way into his bones. The bold one spoke, blessed in courage, and gave his answer:
"I will tell you that pain has touched me. Aching entered me in this dark night and unlocked the body's hoard. My limbs grow heavy, afflicted by pains.

This house of the soul, this doomed body of flesh, must remain in its resting-bed of death, fixed in its bed and covered by an earthen dwelling, the limbs covered with clay. The warrior draws near, and he is not slow in his sport.
The delay before my soul departs will be no longer than seven nights of appointed time, so that on the eighth day, as it moves on, my life will seek its end here.

when my days on the earthly way have glided past and sorrow has lessened, and afterwards I may receive rewards before the knees of the Lord, fresh gifts, and from then on follow God's Lamb in everlasting joys forever;
Now my spirit is eager to go there, eager for the journey. Now you know fully how my limbs will be parted from life. This waiting in the life of the world is long."
Then there was weeping and lamentation, sadness in the young man's heart and mourning in his mind, after he heard that the holy one was ready to depart.

Because of that sudden news about his lord he carried sorrow of mind, heavy at heart. His breast grew dark within, and his mind was troubled with grief, because he saw that his lord was eager to go elsewhere.

He could not restrain himself. Suffering grief, he let hot tears pour and the drops well up like waves. Fate could not keep life, that precious treasure, in the doomed man any longer than had been decreed for him.

The holy one perceived the drooping spirit of the sad-hearted man. Then the protector of his followers, glad of mind and dear to God, began to comfort his disciple and speak to his dearest friend: "Do not be sad, though this sickness burns within me.
It is not hard for me to endure the will of the Lord, my Lord. In this time of sickness I have no sorrow in my mind about death, and I do not greatly fear the war-band of hell's servants.

The firstborn of deceit cannot fasten sin or crime upon me, or any sin of the body. Instead they must lament their pain in the flame, seethed in surging sorrows. They must weep over their exile, cut off from what they desire in that hall of death, deprived of every good thing, of love and of joy.

My dear child, do not be too sick at heart. I am ready for the journey, to take the upward path, eager for rewards in the eternal joy, to see the Lord of victories in return for my former deeds, my beloved child.

It is no torment or struggle for me to seek the God of glory, the King of heaven, where there is peace and bliss, the joy of the glorious, and the Lord present. In this dreary time I eagerly pleased him with spiritual mysteries and with deeds, with mind and strength.
I know that reward to be free of sin, a reward without end, holy on high. My hope urges me to seek it there; my soul hastens from the body's vessel to that lasting joy in blessed riches.
This homeland causes me neither pain nor sorrow. I know for myself that after my body falls I will have an everlasting reward."

Then the glorious kinsman, the brave counsellor, stopped speaking. He was weary in mind and needed rest. The sky darkened over the children of men, and the hours of night glided on, dark over the people.
Then came the day on which the Living One, in the body, the eternal Almighty, brought about the resurrection, the Lord with joy,
when he, the Power, rose from death and from the earth at Eastertide; the Majesty of all majesties raised the greatest of throngs to heaven when he came up from hell.
So in that noble time, on the bright day, the blessed man, exulting in joys, gentle and temperate, summoned his strength with difficulty and with courage.
Then the joy of men rose as quickly as he could, hardy and wise of mind, but weary because of his great afflictions.

Then he began to strengthen his mind with bright faith. Deep in thought, he offered sacrifice by spiritual mysteries in God's temple, according to the Lord's will, and to his servant he began, as was fitting for the lord, [?]
...through the gift of the spirit, to preach the gospel, to speak with signs of victory, and to strengthen his heart with wonders, for glory in the beautiful creation and for blessed prosperity,
so that never in all his life, before or since, in this passing time, did he hear any other teaching like it, or hear the Lord's mystery explained so deeply by a human mouth from a spacious mind.
It seemed truer to him that these were the words of a heavenly angel from the joys of the sky, far more the words of a mighty servant, than the teaching of any man, of men over the earth.
To him it seemed the greatest of wonders that such skill in wisdom should dwell here in the breast of any man among the children of men,
so profound were all his words and wisdom, and the man's conduct, his mind and strength, which the Ruler of angels, the helper of souls, had given him.
Four days in number had then passed by during which the Lord's thegn waited with courage, afflicted by sickness and tormented by pains.
He did not carry sorrow in a sad heart, or a dreary mind, over the parting of the spirit. Death drew near, advancing with stealthy steps, strong and fierce; it sought the soul's house.
The seventh day came upon men, since the hot, flickering rush of arrows in showers of battle had sunk into him near the heart and unlocked his life-hoard, sought out with cunning keys.

Then the wise man, the servant, the attendant thegn, went to visit the noble one at the holy house. There he found his lord, sick and lying down, ready for the journey forth, holy in spirit in God's temple, seething with surging pains.
It was then the sixth hour, at midday; his liege lord's last day was then at hand.
Pressed hard by grievous afflictions, struck down by deadly darts, he could [?] not draw up breath or raise the sound of courageous speech.

Then the servant, sad in mind, chilled and weary of spirit, began to address the one ready to depart, the weary but glad-hearted one, and asked him by the Creator of powers, if he could still command his speech,
to raise his voice so that he might tell him in words, reveal to him in the course of his speech, how he regarded his prospects and his condition in that dark sickness, before death claimed him.
The blessed man gave him answer, a dear man to a dear one, though he could only slowly draw breath, the warrior hardy in courage:

"My dear child, it is not very far now to the very last day of the forced parting, so you must hear my words and my teaching for the last time in this worldly life, never deprived of rewards, and not for long after this.
"Keep well all the pledge and the friendship, the words that we two spoke, dearest of men." "Never, lord, will I let the bond of love fail you in your need!"
"Be ready for the journey once body and limbs and the spirit of this life sever their union through the parting of life.
After that, hurry to tell my sister, the dearest one, about my departure on the long way to the fairer joy, into the eternal dwelling. Also make this known to her in my words, [?]

...that I kept myself from her sight the whole time of my life in the world, because I desired that we two might see each other again in eternal joy, in the glory of heaven, before the face of the eternal Judge, free of sins.
There our love shall abide steadfast, where we two may forever enjoy delights in that bright city, bliss among the angels.
Tell her also to commit this vessel of bones to the hill and enclose the soulless body in clay in the dark chamber, where it must afterwards stay for a time in the house of sand."
Then the attendant's mind was greatly troubled and weighed down with distress by his lord's words, when he quickly realized that his lord's parting from life, his last day, was not far off.
Then he quickly began to speak in words to his friend and lord: "I beseech you, dearest of men of the human race, by the Guardian of souls, that you ease the sorrow of my heart, joy of men.
Your end is not far off, from what I have perceived in your utterances.
Often my sad spirit has been troubled with cares, hot at my heart, my mind mourning, oppressed at night, and I never dared to ask you, father, my comfort.
"Always, when the gem of heaven, men's candle of joy, sank in the west, the sky-bright sun eager for its setting at eventide, I heard another with you, a companion in counsel. [?]"

Sad in mind, I have heard a lord's words, those of an unknown messenger often visiting you, between dawn and the dark night, the speech of a man, and likewise in the morning, the speech of a spirit, of a wise one in your dwelling.
Truly, I do not yet know, unless you, my lord, tell me more in your own words, from where his comings are."
Then the blessed man, renowned for courage, gave answer to his dear one after a long while, as he could only slowly control his breath:
"Lo, you address me with words, my friend, you ask me, who am ready to depart, about something that never before in my life would I make known to any man on earth,
"[?] to any man among the people except to you now, so that men and women would not marvel at it, and in mockery [?] pour it out, and tell of me in songs while I was still living."
Truly, I did not wish through boastful speech to deprive my spirit of its comfort, nor ever to bring upon myself the anger of my Father, the wrath of God.

"Always, ever since I first began to live in this hermitage, in the second year, my Lord of victory, the life-giver of peoples, has sent to me a holy spirit, a heavenly angel, who every [?], the mighty servant of the Creator, [?]"

and in the morning again, triumphant, he sought me out and healed every pain and sorrow of mind for me, and the glorious, gracious messenger locked within my breast the gift of wisdom, far more manifold than any man may know here in this life,

which I am not permitted to make known to any living person of the human race on earth, so that no man could hide from me what he secretly planned in his mind, in the thoughts of his heart, once he came into my sight.
Always, in my mind, I concealed the Lord's glorious coming from every man until this day.
"Dearest of men, now, for your love and for the fellowship that we two kept for so long, I will never let you become sad after my death, weary and sick at heart, seething with surging sorrows."
I will always keep peace with you. Now the soul hastens from the enclosure of the breast to the true joy.

The time is not slow. This vessel of bones is growing weak, the hoard of earth mourns, the spirit hurries itself toward the eternal dwelling, eager to depart to better seats. Now I am greatly wearied by pain."
Then he sank against the wall and bowed his head, but he still kept courage within. Now and then he drew breath, brave in his strength, and the sweetest of fragrances came from his mouth.
As in summertime flowering plants, flowing with honey and fixed firmly in their places, give off a delightful scent throughout the fields, so the saint's breath rose up all day long until evening.

Then the noble radiance went to its setting. The northern sky grew dark and dusky under the clouds. Mist covered the world, and it was covered in darkness. Night pressed over [?] the adornments of the land.

Then the greatest of lights came, holy from the heavens, shining clearly and brightly over the town's halls. The one who had to wait, blessed in courage, awaited his last day, struck by deadly arrows.
A radiance of glory, noble around the noble one, shone brightly clad all night long. The shadows faded away, dissolved under the sky.
The bright gleam was around the holy house, a heavenly candle, from evening twilight until the radiance of dawn came from the east over the deep sea-way, a warm sign of the weather.
The glorious son arose, blessed and mindful of courage, and spoke to his attendant, glorious, to his faithful companion:

"It is time for you to go. Keep all the errands in mind and carry them out quickly, as I commanded you before: the message to the beloved one. Now the spirit, eager for the joys of God, is very ready to leave the body."

Then he raised his hands, fed with the Eucharist, humble through the noble gift. He also opened his eyes, the holy gems of the head, and looked up to the kingdom of the heavens, glad at heart, toward the rewards of grace. And then he sent forth his spirit, made beautiful by his deeds, into the joy of glory.
Then Guthlac's spirit was led, blessed, on the upward way. Angels carried it to the long-lasting joy. The body grew cold, lifeless under the sky. Then a light shone there, the brightest of beams.

That whole beacon, a heavenly radiance, was around the holy house, rising from the earth like a fiery tower raised straight up to the roof of the heavens. It was seen under the sky, brighter than the sun and than the beauty of the noble stars.
Hosts of angels sang a victory song. The sound was heard in the air under the heavens, the joy of the saints.
So the dwelling place, the blessed man's ancestral seat, was filled with bliss, with sweet scents and heavenly wonders, and with the voices of angels, all through its interior.

How the scent and the sound, the heavenly voice and the holy song, the high majesty of God, were heard there, clamor after clamor, was more wonderful and more delightful than any voice in the world could tell.

The island trembled and the ground heaved. Then the messenger grew afraid, robbed of courage. The man, unhappy, left in haste and boarded the boat. The wave-horse drove on, the rusher over the water went, swift beneath sorrows.

The sky shone hot, bright over the town halls. The sea-wood hurried on, light and eager for its course. The water-steed sped laden to the harbor, so that the sea-floater, after its play in the waves, struck the sandy shore and ground against the gravel.

The one who knew he must stay behind after his lord, his dear friend, had departed this life carried grieving sorrow, hot at heart, with a sad mind and a weary spirit. The sound of weeping painfully stirred him.
Tears welled up in waves, hot drops on his cheeks, and in his breast he carried great sorrow of mind. He had to bring the message to the maiden, hateful news, in truth.

Then, cold at heart, he came to where the woman was, the beloved kinswoman in glory. He did not hide what had happened, the departure of the dying man. Bereft of his friend, he sang a song of departure and spoke these words:
"Courage is best for the one who must most often endure the loss of a lord, and think deeply on the hardship of parting from his lord when the time comes, woven by the decrees of fate.
He knows this who must grieve, sad at heart, who knows that his loyal treasure-giver is buried. He must go away from there humbled and mournful.
He lacks joy who most often endures hardships in a sorrowful mind. Truly, I have little cause to laugh at this departure from life.
My lord, the leader of men, your brother, the best man born of the human race, from childhood on, between the two seas, of all those we have ever heard of among the English,

the support of the weary, the joy of his dear kinsmen, the protector of friends, has departed from worldly joys to God's judgment, into the majesty of glory, to seek the dwellings of the homeland on the upward way.

Now the earthly part, the broken bone-house, lies in its bed of death within the dwellings, and the glorious part has gone out of the body's vessel into the light of God to seek the reward of victory,

and he told me to say to you that the two of you may always share a home together with that peaceful company in the eternal joy, the glorious reward for your deeds, and enjoy glory and bliss as you wish.
"My Lord of victory also ordered me, when he was ready for his journey, to tell you, dearest of women, to cover his body with earth."
"Now you know at once about my journey. I must go away sorrowful at heart, humbled in mind, with my spirit drooping."
